newsitem.title: USA: British Telecom deal would cap 28-year MCI saga.
newsitem.headline: British Telecom deal would cap 28-year MCI saga.

text.p: A merger between MCI Communications Corp. and British Telecommunications Plc would cap a 28-year history of MCI's hammering at the long-distance market once dominated by AT&T Corp.

Founded by Bill McGowan in 1968 as MICOM, or Microwave Communications of America Inc., the company was the first to be authorised by the Federal Communications Commission to compete against AT&T in the domestic long-distance market.
MCI, now the nation's second-biggest long-distance company, started offering service between Chicago and St. Louis in January 1972. It sold stock and was incorprated as MCI Communications in 1973.
During much of the next decade MCI's battles with AT&T were like David struggling against Goliath.
Washington-based MCI filed an antitrust suit against AT&T in 1974 and six years later, a jury ruled in MCI's favour on almost all counts and awarded the company $1.8 billion.

But it was the 1982 agreement between the Justice Department and AT&T for AT&T to sell off the regional Bell phone companies that radically changed MCI's prospects along with the telephone industry at large.

MCI said the breakup of AT&T eventually led to its purchase of Western Union International Inc., part of a global expansion that transformed MCI into a major long-distance competitor alongside AT&T and Sprint Corp.
By 1988, MCI claimed to have 10 percent of the total long-distance market and had more than doubled its annual revenue to about $5.1 billion.

MCI launched a series of new products, made acquisitions and forged alliances in the early 1990s, including the launch of its Friends & Family savings plan and a $1 billion venture with News Corp. Ltd. on media and satellite projects.
When founder McGowan died of a heart attack in 1992, the company named Bert Roberts to the chairman's post.

In 1993, MCI and British Telecom set a strategic alliance, with British Telecom investing $4.3 billion for a 20 percent stake in MCI. MCI said Friday it was in talks for British Telecom to acquire the rest of MCI in a deal analysts said could be worth about $22.1 billion.
The two companies started Concert, a venture that provides global communications services for business customers.

Through its recent expansion into the Internet market and wireless communications, MCI now has about 20 percent of the long-distance market. Last year it earned $548 million on revenues of $15.27 billion.
